question: to the Commission Ciaran Mullooly (Renew) Subject:

It has been brought to my attention that the Department of Housing and building control authorities in Ireland are refusing to recognise or accept technical certificates for modern methods of construction (MMC) products (specifically cladding) issued by Kiwa, an inspection and certification company accredited in other EU Member States. Despite the products holding valid certification demonstrating compliance with safety and performance standards equivalent to those required by the National Standards Authority of Ireland (NSAI), developers are being forced to undergo redundant, costly and time-consuming national recertification. 1.

Is the Commission aware that local building control authorities in Ireland are effectively disregarding certificates from accredited EU notified bodies, thereby creating a de facto technical barrier to trade?
Does the Commission consider the systematic refusal to accept equivalent certifications from other Member States a violation of Regulation (EU) 2019/515 on the mutual recognition of goods1?
What steps will the Commission take to ensure that Irish authorities comply with the single market rules to prevent the delay of innovative, sustainable MMC products?
OJ L 91, 29.3.2019, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2019/515/oj.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.7.2026) The Commission is not aware of any practice of Irish building control authorities of not taking into account certificates issued by notified bodies in other EU Member States. To assess whether there are grounds for an investigation, the Commission would need more information about the products in question. Under Regulation (EU) 3110/20241, if a product is covered by a harmonised technical specification, it must be CE-marked and Member States are required to allow it onto their markets. If a product is not covered by either a harmonised specification or a European technical assessment (ETA), the placing of the product on the market is governed by national frameworks and the principle of mutual recognition. In the case of non-harmonised or partially harmonised products, Regulation (EU) 2019/515 on mutual recognition2 requires the competent authorities of the Member State of destination to take account of test reports and certificates issued by conformity assessment bodies. Competent authorities may not refuse such reports or certificates on grounds related to the competence of the body where it is accredited in accordance with Regulation (EC) No 765/20083 for the relevant assessment activity. The Commission is not aware of instances where Irish authorities systematically fail to give consideration to certificates issued by accredited bodies in other Member States. With the Construction Product Regulation (CPR) Acquis process, the Commission aims to update, by 2033, all harmonised standards developed over the last 25 years and to extend coverage to all relevant product families4. Further details about the process are laid down in the (First) CPR Working Plan for 2026-20295.
